parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: reading flux values from Phi-x graph
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at Fig. 10.2 between $x = 0$ and $x = 3.0\text{ cm}$. Read off the flux per turn at each end and think about why a 40-turn coil needs the number of turns included as well as the change per turn.
parts.proper_answer: Change in flux linkage $= N\Delta\Phi = 40 \times (5.0 - 3.0) \times 10^{-6} = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Wb}$ (magnitude).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Flux From Flux Linkage**
You are sitting with two ideas here. $\Phi$ is the flux through one turn, read from the graph in $10^{-6}\text{ Wb}$. Flux linkage is the total linkage for the whole coil, so it is $N$ times larger because each of the 40 turns links the flux.

Step 2: **Read The Graph And Calculate**
From Fig. 10.2, at $x = 0$, $\Phi = 5.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Wb}$ and at $x = 3.0\text{ cm}$, $\Phi = 3.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Wb}$. So the change per turn is: $$\Delta\Phi = (5.0 - 3.0) \times 10^{-6} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Wb}$$ For $N = 40$: $$\Delta(N\Phi) = 40 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Wb}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: relation of speed to time and distance
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the induced e.m.f. tells you. It is set by how fast the flux linkage is changing, so a known e.m.f. together with your known total change from (a)(i) can tell you how long the motion took.
Hint 2: Once you have the time, use the distance travelled, $3.0\text{ cm}$, to get the constant speed. Remember to convert cm to m before dividing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Faraday's Law To Find The Time**
Faraday's law says the magnitude of induced e.m.f. equals rate of change of flux linkage: $$|E| = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$ You know $|E| = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V}$ and $\Delta(N\Phi) = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Wb}$ from (a)(i). Rearrange for time first: $$\Delta t = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{|E|}$$ $$\Delta t = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-5}}{5.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.16\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Convert Distance To Speed**
The coil moves at constant speed over $\Delta x = 3.0\text{ cm} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ in that time: $$v = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$$ $$v = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{-2}}{0.16} = 0.19\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This makes sense: a small flux change per second gives a small e.m.f., so the coil must be moving slowly.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: e.m.f. proportional to gradient of flux
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the shape of Fig. 10.2. It is made of two straight-line sections meeting at $x = 3\text{ cm}$. With constant speed, think about what a constant slope of $\Phi$ against $x$ means for $\Phi$ against $t$ and therefore for the induced e.m.f.
Hint 2: Compare the two sections. Look at whether $\Phi$ is falling or rising with $x$, and compare how steep each section is to decide on relative sign and size of $E$.
parts.proper_answer: Two horizontal non-zero levels: constant $E$ from 0 to 3 cm and a different constant $E$ from 3 to 6 cm. The 3 to 6 cm level has opposite sign to the 0 to 3 cm level and larger magnitude.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why The E.m.f. Is Constant On Each Section**
At constant speed $v$, rate of change with time is proportional to rate of change with distance: $$E = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = -Nv\frac{d\Phi}{dx}$$ So $E$ follows the gradient $d\Phi/dx$ of Fig. 10.2. A straight line has constant gradient, so $E$ is constant while the coil is on that section.

Step 2: **Decide Sign And Size**
From $x = 0$ to $3\text{ cm}$, $\Phi$ decreases with $x$, so the gradient is negative and $E$ has one polarity. From $x = 3$ to $6\text{ cm}$, $\Phi$ increases with $x$, so the gradient is positive and $E$ reverses sign. The rise from 3 to 6 cm is steeper than the fall from 0 to 3 cm, about twice as steep, so $|E|$ is larger on the second section. Sketch two flat lines on opposite sides of the $E = 0$ axis with a sudden jump at $x = 3\text{ cm}$.
